column40:
Initials of George Daniel on upper side of cover. On H3v is written in a seventeenth-century hand, "Anagr. { Elisabeth Rotton / Her lot is to b neat. }" There are annotations for performance throughout in a seventeenth-century hand. Tiffany Stern points to Elisabeth Rotton's burial plaque, in St Laurence Church, Meriden, Warwickshire, which reads: "Anagr. { Elisabeth Rotton / I to a blest Throne }". She also demonstrates that Malone owned or borrowed this copy for some time, since he refers to its added directions for music in his 1780 "Supplement".

Signature of George Steevens on the title page, and a few notes by him in the text; this copy was possibly lot 1299 in the Steevens sale by King, 21 May 1800. Bookstamp of the Duke of Roxburghe on the title page; sold as lot 3860 in the Roxburghe sale by Evans, 6 June 1812. This copy was later owned by the Marquis of Blandford, and in his sale (White Knights library) by Evans, 30 June 1819, it was lot 3957.

This copy also appears, as an anonymous property, in a sale by Evans, 25-29 January 1830, lot 796. It was then owned by George Daniel, whose monogram is stamped on the cover; in his sale by Sotheby's, 26 July 1864, it was lot 1430. The Huth copy (with bookplate) acquired by Mr. Cochran in November 1911 prior to the public sale. Gift of Alexander S. Cochran, December 1911.

From the Christie's catalogue: "[Thomas Betterton (1635-1710), copy almost certainly prepared for him acting Hamlet] early manuscript notes and marking in the text – Donald and Mary Hyde (1909-66 and 1912-2003; bookplate; Mary Hyde Eccles sale, Christie’s NY, 14 April 2004, lot 78) – Roberto Salinas Price (d. 2012, Mexican bibliophile and businessman, his collection sold via Heritage Book Shop; ‘Biblioteca Huicalco’ tooled at spine foot of box)."
column43: From Christie's catalogue: "Contemporary manuscript annotations, Hamlet’s lines marked with a stroke, 60 text emendations amendments ranging from a single word (‘A’ for ‘He’, ‘I’m’ for ‘I am’) to a longer insertion: ‘O Good Horatio, Ile take the Ghosts word for a Thousand pounds. Did perceive.’, a few deletions, cuts marked .... The present copy is clearly annotated for the part of Hamlet, with each line marked in the margin with a stroke and with a number of changes – text amendments and line cuts affecting only Hamlet’s lines – written in a contemporary hand. Theatre companies would own a set of plays to be used by the principal actors to learn their parts for performance. The present copy, almost certainly annotated for and used by Betterton, would have been owned and prepared by the company, very possibly by John Downes, prompter and long-term member of Betterton’s company. It is closely associated with a rehearsal copy of the 1676 quarto edition at the Folger Library ... which is also marked for the part of Hamlet and with some of the same textual amendments; it is also very similarly bound in marbled wrappers. The only other rehearsal or prompt copy of Hamlet to survive from the 17th century is the Smock Alley copy of the Third Folio (now at the University of Edinburgh) annotated c. 1680."

If you could have only one quarto, I am glad it is an undated 'Julius Caesar' for I have studied that play bibliographically for two years and am sending you under separate cover the results of my research. My opinion as to the arrangement of editions was approved by Messrs. W. A. White, Beverly Chew and L.S. Livingston here as well as Mr. Pollard and Mr. H. B. Wheatley in England although we are none of us sure as to 'Quarto 5'. [inserted in pencil] ^the one of 60pp. considerably later than mine^  All I know is that none of them could have been printed before 1682 and I think '5' comes after the 1684 one. I am naturally very anxious to see your copy and make a careful examination for the the Census as well as for my own satisfaction. If you would be so very kind as to bring it over to town with you and then let me come down to your office and examine it, I should be much grateful. If you would prefer to bring it up here, I will borrow Mr. White's copies when I go over there on Tuesday next and we can make it absolutely certain as to which edition it belonged to. If it's not too much trouble and you would call me up on the phone (5360 Spring) any morning this week before 12 o'clock, I could arrange about Mr. White's books as it's so much better to make the physical comparison. I shall be out Monday and Tuesday of next week but any time after that will suit me and I will gladly go to you if that suits you better. New copies of 'Julius Caesar' are like glittering El Dorados to me now. Hoping you will be interested too, I am truly yours, Henrietta C. Bartlett."

column40: It is almost certain that this volume comes from the collection of the English Jesuit college of Saint-Omer. The name "Nevill" has been written in ink on the current first page, possibly the pseudonym of Basil Thomas Scarisbrick, then Eccleston (1713? -1789), educated in Saint-Omer around 1727, and who gave a series of works to his old school in 1736. Every 100 pages approximately, the initials "PS" were printed using an awl. Identified in 2014 by librarian Rémy Cordonnier in the public library at Saint-Omer, having been assumed previously—in part due to missing preliminary leaves—to be an 18th-century edition (SW).

column40: The bookplate found at the front of this volume dates to c 1740 and therefore most likely belonged to Wadham Wyndham (d. 1736). After Wyndham’s death it is not known what happened to the Folio. As some point it was acquired by Francis Fortescue Urquhart (1868–1934). Urquhart sold the Folio through Sotheby’s 598, 26 March 1923. At the sale, the volume was purchased by Quaritch for £260. Quaritch then turned around and sold it to Henry Folger for $1,275 that same month.

column40: The Folio was bequeathed to Isaac Reed by John Henderson, and given to Reed by Henderson’s widow on 3rd February 1786, as documented in a MS inscription in the Comedies volume. It was later sold to a ‘JW’ for £38 (Lot 8663) in the sale of Reed’s library in 1807. Correspondence dated from 1807 in the Bute Collection at Mount Stuart notes that John Stuart, 4th Earl and 1st Marquess of Bute (1744-1814), thought the Folio in Reed’s 1807 sale was ‘too dear’. The Bute F1 was owned by John Crichton-Stuart, 3rd Marquess of Bute (1847-1900) and is listed in the Catalogue of the Library at St. John’s Lodge, Regent’s Park, London in 1896. This suggests that the First Folio likely joined the Bute Collection at some point during the 19th century and was acquired by either the 1st, 2nd, or 3rd Marquess of Bute.

column43: This copy features extensive early annotations by someone who apparently knew some of the actors in the King's Men, Shakespeare's company, and had seen them perform. On the list of principal actors (sig. πA6) the annotator claims to 'know' Robert Benfield, John Lowine 'by eyewitness', and Richard Burbage 'by report'. Beneath William Shakespeare is the intriguing comment 'Leass for making' (perhaps meaning that he, as the maker of plays, may have acted less than other actors). Other annotations record responses to the first few plays in the volume: 'stark naught' for Two Gentlemen of Verona, 'pretty well' for The Tempest, and 'very good, light' for Merry Wives. The annotator characterizes Ford's mistrust of his wife in the latter play as 'a good jealous man's dilemma.' Passages throughout are marked with 'ap.' -- presumably an abbreviation of 'approbo' (I approve).

Also known as the "Halliwell-Phillipps Unique Proof" (though now known not to be unique) and the "Lilly Proof." Removed from Halliwell-Phillipps volume labeled "The proof engraving of Droeshout’s portrait of Shakespeare, 1623." Encapsulated with a note in Halliwell-Phillipps’ hand that reads: "This engraving belonged to an imperfect copy of the First Folio that was purchased by Lilly at a sale at Sotheby’s on 11 May, 1863, lot 110, and I bought the engraving itself of Lilly exactly a year afterwards, 11 May, 1864, for one hundred guineas." That copy of the First Folio (West 39) is now owned by the Royal Shakspeare Theatre and kept by the Shakespeare Birthplace Trust at the Shakespeare Centre Library. Only four impressions of state 1 are known: one at the British Library (c.39.k.15), one at the Bodleian (Arch. G.c.8) and two at the Folger (ART Box D783 no.1 and STC 22273 Fo.1 no.02, title page).

column43: Note from a Folger curator on front flyleaf, dated "17 Sep. 58": "The loose leaf, uncorrected, but without proofreader's marks, clearly came at some time from what is now Folio 79. Was the extraction made before H.C.F. bought 79? By Halliwell-Phillipps?'  Longer note (by Halliwell-Phillipps?) on previous front flyleaf: "This unique printer's proof of a page of the first folio Edition of Shakespeare is of remarkable interest in connexion with the question of the care bestowed upon the printing of that celebrated volume, & hence its relative authority. The corrections are restricted to a single page, the other side of hte leaf corresponding with the ordinary copies; so that the page here shown is probably a revise of a corrected proof, this particular portion having, for some reason, escaped revision with the rest. It was found in a parcel of fragments of the first folio in my possession, but the most anxious search failed in the discovery of any other page similarly treated. The corrections in the second column are the most interesting, especially those which show that the original corrector of the press paid great attention to the punctuation. Thus in line 11, the comma is removed from its position after the word *that* to its proper localis(?) - after the word *horse*; in line 25, a comma improperly introduced is marked for omission; & in line 52, another is correctly inserted after the word *speake*. The corrections in line 17 are curious. The compositor had spelt *rheume* without the letters *he*, which the corrector inserts, but the latter, not wishing to run the line over, takes out two superfluous letters in other words. The careful mode in which this page is corrected will perhaps do something to increase the authority of the first folio. Thus, in the seventh line of the second column, the passage, "at the full of tide", originally printed, "at the of full tide", is carefully altered. Some editors consider that the reading of the second folio, "at full of tide", is correct but it is reasonable to suppose that had the MS. wanted the particle *the*, the same careful hand would have marked it for omission."

column40: Charles I copy, with his signature ("CR"); presented by the King to Sir Thomas Herbert (1606-82); probably in the collection of Richard Mead (1673-1754); probably purchased at his sale (lot 1744, 7 May 1755) by Anthony Askew (1722-74); purchased at his sale (lot 347, 14 February 1775) by George Steevens (1736-1800); purchased at his sale (lot 1314, 21 May 1800) for the Royal Library during the reign of George III (r. 1760-1820); George Steevens annotated the fly-leaf to note that Thomas Herbert had been Master of the Revels to Charles I. When the book was sold at the sale of Steevens's library in 1800, it was purchased for the Royal Library by George III. Reading the annotation about Herbert, the King noticed that Steevens had erred, so he also annotated the book to record that Herbert had in fact been Charles I's Groom of the Bedchamber.

column40: Came to the University as part of the “Bibliothek des Frey-Grynaeischen Instituts”. The Frey-Grynaean Institute was founded by Johann Ludwig Frey, whose great-grandfather, one Johann Jakob Frey (1606–1636), spent a considerable amount of his life in England and from whose possessions the Second Folio came to Basel. It is unclear whether the ex libris “EX. BIBLIOTH. IOH. IACOBI FREY. BASIL.” on the inside of the Folio’s cover refers to the original Johann Jakob Frey or his son of the same name who inherited his father’s collection. Johann Ludwig Frey inherited the collections left to him by his father including the Second Folio and added them to the library in the Frey-Grynaean Institute. In 1909 the Second Folio as rediscovered when a large part of the Frey-Grynaean library collection were transferred to the University Library for security, among other reasons.

column38: From dealer catalogue: "a few small damp stains to margins, 5 tiny holes to the first page of The Comedy of Errors (with slight loss of 3 letters of text), a couple of short closed marginal tears, a little slight soiling and browning .... Lacking the initial leaf, To the Reader, but with all other leaves present and mostly intact. The first 17 and last 19 leaves have been neatly repaired (not recently), with some loss of the ruled border and/or varying degrees of minor text loss to 25 of those leaves, usually only a few words or less to the last few lines. The title and colophon pages have both been laid down, and there is some loss of the imprint at the foot of the title page, including almost all of the date. (The text that remains is: London, Printed by Tho. Cotes, for William Aspley, and are [...] of the Parrat in Pauls Church-yard. 1...). The inner margin of the final leaf has loss of much of the ruled border, portions of each of the last 17 lines of text (usually only a couple of words per line), and the beginning of the two-line colophon: the first word of line one, and part of the initial 'R' from the first word of line two. The five publisher's names and, most importantly, the 1632 date are all intact. The title page portrait of Shakespeare by Martin Droeshout is in the third state, with the tiny difference in the highlighting of the eyes and the extra strand of hair to the right side of the coiffure. The letter 'M' is missing from the artist's name, but the portrait is complete and a fine impression."

column40: Formerly the property of St. Alban’s College (the English College), Valladolid, Spain; Lee names the censor as Guillén Sanchez rather than Guillermo Sánchez, misreading the censor’s signature ("Gulielmum" for "Guilielmum").  Otherwise, the English Jesuit William Sankey has been nominated as the censor, but the hand of the censor’s certificate is apparently Spanish.
column43: Copy bears (on title page) the certificate of a censor for the Inquisition ("Opus auctoritate Sancti officij permissum et expurgatum eadem auctoritate per Guilielmum Sanchaeum e Socte Jesu") and marks of censorship.  M. for M. (F1 recto-G6 verso) has been completely excised.  Passages are obliterated in Temp. (A1 recto and A5 recto), Much Ado (K3 recto and K6 verso), LLL (L5 recto and verso, L6 recto, M2 recto, and M3 recto), Merch. (P2 recto), AYL (R3 verso), All’s Well (V4 verso), John (a5 recto and verso and b5 recto), 1 Hen. IV (e4 verso), 1 Hen. VI (l6 recto), 2 Hen. VI (o1 recto and o2 recto), Hen. VIII (x2 verso, x4 recto, x5 recto, y3 recto, y5 verso, and y6 recto and verso), Troilus (2b4 recto), Ham. (2q4 recto), and Lear (2s6 verso). Earlier spine removed to curatorial file. Port. (on title page) in state 3. Some plays are designated "good" in an 18th-century hand in their caption, Merry Wives (D2 recto), Errors (H1 recto), Much Ado (I3 recto), and Merch. (04 recto), and likewise Cymb. is designated "rare" (3b1 recto).  Passages in Macb. are marked by adjacent pencil strokes (2o4 recto, b27-29, and 2o5 verso, a49-53).  Other manuscript additions include the inscription "Collegii Sancti Albani Anglorum Vallisoleti" ([superscript pi]A3 recto) and the signature with rubric "Joannes Luca S.J." (*2 recto), possibly that of the English Jesuit John Lucas. See Sidney Lee, "Shakespeare and the Inquisition: A Spanish Second Folio," in his, Elizabethan and Other Essays (1929), 184-95, first published 1922.  Lee cites most of the obliterations and manuscript additions although not always fully or accurately.  (Full list of obliterations and manuscript additions on file.)

Either leaf f1 or f6 (watermarked redundantly) is supplied from another copy; probably f1 (touched up with pen and ink on the recto). Received in 1942 by MacLeish from Halifax on behalf of the Gill family, given “to help the Empire war effort” and “presented to the United States of America as a mark of the gratitude of the ordinary people of England for all they have done and are doing.” MacLeish notes the folio is a “symbol of the common ties of language and particularly of poetry which bind our peoples together at this hour of their common trial—their common struggle for the freedom of men, and above all, the freedom of men’s minds.” Given in April 1882 by Margaret D'Aubney Hanson, widow of Samuel Hanson (1804–1883), to Thomas Hornblower Gill; subsequently inherited by Ernest Compton Gill and Ernest Walter Brudenell Gill. Also inscribed: "Thomas Dove, 1706"; "Cormelian"; "William Love"; and illegible note dated 1787.

column38: Title page in facsimile; Contains a letter from F. G. Kenyon (Dept of manuscripts, British Museum) to Dr Leeper, discussing this edition of Shakespeare (June 9th 1904): 'Dear Sir, Your Shakespeare arrived two days ago considerably later than your letter on the subject. One of my colleagues in the department of Printed Books has examined it carefully, and he reports that it is as you have always supposed, a copy of the Second Folio, with the exception of the last leaf, which is from the Third Folio. You will notice that the top outer corner of this leaf has been torn off, do doubt in order to conceal the fact that the pagination did not correspond with that of the rest of the volume. About half of the preliminary matter is wanting, the most important leaves being among those which have disappeared. Of course this would affect the pecunary value of the book very considerably, and my colleague remarks that the £50 for which the book was insured is probably quite as much as it it worth". I mention this, not because I suppose you would wish to sell the volume, or because it real value as evidence for the text of Shakespeare is in any way affected, but merely because the deatil may be of interest to you. I am returning the book separately as an insured parcel. Yours sincerely, F.S. Kenyon)'

From auction catalogue: "The initials 'S.P.' on the spine have not been positively identified. Even though his Diary records the purchase of an edition of Shakespeare's plays in 1664, later sold when he acquired the newly-published Fourth Folio, Pepys used a monogram rather than initials as a mark of ownership, and in the absence of a shelf mark there is no evidence to identify 'S.P.' with Samuel Pepys. It seems improbable that these initials stand for Sir Philip Sydenham (1676-1739), the third and last Baronet of Brympton, as he was not born early enough to be the first owner of this copy, and the binding itself is unlikely to be any later than 1690."

Jaggard, after he set up that business in Stratford in 1909). A pencilled note on the free front endpaper above the bookplate (written ca. 1928 by the E. Thompson who also handled the sale of Jaggard's First Folio in that year) states that "this copy has been in possession of the Jaggard family for generations. It was used as a stage prompt copy during the eighteenth century and has many hundreds of interesting pencil annotations in the margins", though the annotations look closer to 19th c.; in 1972 correspondence concerning this copy (among gifts from the same donors), Michael Papantonio (Seven Gables Bookshop) remarked that "Jaggard was a trader in Shakespeare materials, bought and sold many copies, and made up copies; and the note that it was in the Jaggard family for generations is, I think at best pretty doubtful." Gift of William V.A. and Georgiana MacArthur Hansen in 1972, together with a copy of the Second Folio and the second quarto of Julius Caesar (1691); the Hansens had already donated, in 1971, a copy of the First Folio (cataloged as Hay Rare PR2751.A1x 1623). All three folios had previously been owned by Mrs. Hansen's father, Alfred MacArthur. See the Josiah record for the First Folio for further notes on the Hansens' connection to Brown University.

column40: From bookseller's catalogue: "Later endpaper cut-out on front pastedown to reveal ownership inscription of George Frere (1774-1854), earlier ownership inscription “E. R. Grant” (Elizabeth Raper Grant), his future wife, to an early blank .... The ownership inscription “M Raper” at the head of the title page of Othello, a smaller, neater hand than the cast list, must be that of one of the silk-trading brothers Moses or Matthew Raper (1680-1748), both directors of the Bank of England, or of the latter’s son, the antiquarian Matthew Raper the younger (1705-1778). On the latter’s death, his manor house at Thorley, Hertfordshire, passed to his brother John, whose granddaughter was Elizabeth Raper Grant (1778-1850), who in 1806 married George Frere (1774-1854); his ownership inscription is retained beneath the cut-out paper on the front pastedown. Matthew Raper the younger, a friend of Benjamin Franklin, was elected to the Royal Society on 30 May 1754 and was awarded the Copley Medal in 1771 for a paper 'Inquiry into the Value of the ancient Greek and Roman Money.'”
column43: From bookseller's catalogue: "annotated with textual comparisons with the first quarto of 1622, and prefaced by a unique manuscript cast list from c.1691-2 naming actors involved in a notorious murder trial with dramatic echoes of Shakespeare’s tragedy .... The textual annotations are interesting, in that they compare the 1655 readings with those of the first quarto of 1622, rather than the folio text published the following year .... The unpublished manuscript cast list written on the blank facing the title is a remarkable survival, written shortly before two key names mentioned in it became embroiled in one of the most lurid murder trials of the age, with startling echoes of Othello. The manuscript evidently names the cast for a revival of the play by the United Company, almost certainly at Drury Lane. The title role is played by the legendary actor-manager Thomas Betterton (1635-1710) .... The cast list here has “Mis Bracegirdle” as Desdemona, “Mis Knight” as Emilia, and “Mis Richerson” as Bianco [sic]. Anne Bracegirdle (1671-1748) had been in the foster care of Betterton and his wife since infancy. Her first recorded performance was 12 January 1688 for the United Company, and she graduated to leading roles around 1689-90. “Mis Knight” is Frances Maria Knight. “Mis Richerson” is Mrs Richardson, whose best attested dates of activity are 1690-92. Playing Roderigo is Mr Alexander, the stage name of John Verbruggen; in the role of Cassio is William Mountfort. The cast list must therefore date between October 1690, when Verbruggen joined the company, and 10 December 1692, when William Mountfort was murdered. Around this time, Anne Bracegirdle was being stalked by an unwanted admirer, Captain Richard Hill. He was jealous of the dashing Mountfort and imagined that Mountfort had captured the actress’s heart. On 9 December 1692 Hill and a companion, Charles, Lord Mohun, attempted to abduct Bracegirdle on her way back from a dinner party. Mountfort came by on his way home and Hill stabbed him. Hill fled to the Isle of Wight and Mohun stood trial before the House of Lords as his accomplice. Frances Maria Knight was among those who gave evidence. Lord Mohun’s acquittal caused a scandal. A journalist was taken into custody for saying the evidence was strong enough to hang a commoner. After Mountfort’s death, his widow married John Verbruggen."

column40:
Note by Malone on endpaper: "This edition of some of Shak-speare’s Poems is so very rare, that I have never seen another copy; nor is it mentioned in any catalogue ancient or modern.
 All the poems from Signature D5 were written by Thomas Heywood, who was so offended at Jaggard for printing them under the name of Shakespeare that he has added a postscript to his Apology for Actors, 4to 1612, on this subject; and Jaggard in consequence of it appears to have printed a new title-page to please Heywood, without the name of Shakespeare in it. The former title page was no doubt intended to [...] be cancelled, but, by some inadvertence, they were both prefixed to this copy, and I have retained them as a curiosity. Heywood thus speaks of this in the postscript above-mentioned: 'Here likewise I must necessarily insert a manifest injury done to me in that worke [Britayne’s Troy] by taking the two epistles of Paris to Helen and Helen to Paris, and printing them in a less volume under the name of another, wch may put the world in opinion I might steale them from him, and hee, to do himselfe right, hath since published them in his owne name; but as I must acknowledge my lines not worthy his patro-nage under whom he hath publisht them, or the author, I know, much offended with Mr Jaggard, that (altogether unknown to him) presumed to make so bold with his name.'
In consequence of Jaggard’s conduct, these translations from Ovid for near a century and a half passed for Shakespeare’s, when at length my friend Dr Farmer, in 1766, pointed out the occasion of the mistake.
                                    E.M.
                                    Octr 22, 1785"
